script.title: Why Paris Hauled Its Dead Into Old Stone Mines
sentences: More than six million people lie in old tunnels under Paris.
None of them were buried there.
By the late 1700s, the Holy Innocents' Cemetery was a two-metre mound packed with centuries of dead.
In 1780, a basement wall next door collapsed under the weight of the mass grave.
Burials inside the city walls were banned after that.
Every night, wagons draped in black cloth carried the bones to a well above the city's old limestone mines.
It took two years to empty most of the cemeteries.
Later, a mine director had skulls and thigh bones stacked into patterns.
script.description:
Paris ran out of room for its dead.
So it moved them into the mines under its own streets.
claims_en: The Catacombs of Paris hold the remains of more than six million people in former stone quarries/mines.
The remains were moved there from cemeteries, not buried there originally.
By the end of the 18th century, the Holy Innocents' Cemetery was a two-metre-high mound of earth filled with centuries of Parisian dead.
On May 31, 1780, a basement wall in a property adjoining the cemetery collapsed under the weight of the mass grave behind it.
All burials within the city walls were forbidden after 1780.
Nightly processions of black cloth-covered wagons carried the dead to a well dug at the Tombe-Issoire, above the renovated mine passageways.
Much of the Left Bank rests on Lutetian limestone that was mined; depleted mines were abandoned.
It took two years to empty the majority of Paris's cemeteries.
From 1810, mine inspection director Héricart de Thury had skulls, femurs and tibias stacked into patterns.
